html:
The first special economic zone of the People's Republic of China, set up in 1980 at Shenzhen, then a small border town of fishing villages and farms across the river from Hong Kong. In a few decades it grew into one of the largest cities in China, with about 18 million people.

It was one of four zones created in 1980 under reform and opening, along with Zhuhai, Shantou and Xiamen. The idea was to test capitalist methods in a fenced-off area without changing the whole country. In the zone, foreign and Hong Kong firms could invest, pay lower taxes, hire workers on contracts and export freely. Land could be leased for money, a first in Communist China.

Why Shenzhen took off:

  • Hong Kong next door had capital, know-how and factories looking for cheap land and labour.
  • Millions of young migrants came from the countryside to work on assembly lines.
  • Success there persuaded doubters in the party. On his southern tour of 1992, Deng Xiaoping praised the zone and pushed for faster reform.

Shenzhen started with cheap assembly, from toys to electronics. Over time it moved up to design and invention. It is home to firms such as Huawei, Tencent and BYD, and its electronics markets make it a centre of world hardware. Its port is one of the busiest container ports in the world. The model of special zones was copied across China and in many other countries, and after China joined the WTO in 2001, the export boom it began went national.
